newsitem.title: USA: Kansas expert grim over wheat prospects after cold.
newsitem.headline: Kansas expert grim over wheat prospects after cold.

text.p: A Kansas agronomist said Monday it will take a "miracle" for the wheat crop in his region to survive after it was blasted by bitter cold temperatures this weekend.

Curtis Thompson, Kansas State University extension agronomist in Garden City, Kan., said the only hope for the crop now is if secondary wheat "tillers," or shoots, can develop into fully-fledged wheat plants in time for harvest.
"We've probably destroyed most of the tillers that are jointed because of the cold temperatures," said Thompson, who covers an area of 24 counties in southwest Kansas.
Thompson said that while primary tillers were destoyed or badly damaged, it might be possible for secondary tillers to make up for some of the loss.

"We're going to have to depend on late tillers that can come on and produce grain. We've seen that happen over the last two years, but we've also had unique weather conditions to allow that to occur," Thompson said.

He estimated that about 75 percent of the wheat in his area was jointed, heading into the weekend cold snap. Thompson said his district traditionally devotes an average of about three million acres to growing wheat.
A wheat plant puts up several tillers as it emerges, but usually only one of those develops a head that eventually produces the plant's valuable grain, Thompson said.

"A plant will adapt to its conditions by putting up more or less tillers. If you kill the leading tillers, they're no longer consuming the nutrients. Then the secondary tiller can kick in and absorb the nutrients," Thompson said.
But Thompson said that in order for such secondary tiller development to occur, abnormally cool, wet weather must prevail during the months of May and June in the flat, open U.S. Plains.

"The worst-case scenario will be if it turns hot going into May and June. Then we'll have real devastation to these developing (secondary tillers)," Thompson said. "It's somewhat ironic after this cold snap, but now we've got to avoid heat for the back end of the wheat crop to allow those late tillers to progress."
On Saturday, temperatures dipped to five degrees Fahrenheit in Goodland, Kan., 10 degrees at Garden City, and 14 at Dodge City, meteorologists said Monday.
By 6:00 p.m. CDT (1800 CDT) Friday, the temperature was down to 12 degrees in Tribune, Kan., and stayed at or below that level until 8 a.m. CDT (0800 CDT) Saturday, Thompson said.
"It just got too cold, too long for this crop to hold out," he said.
